title: Strong convergence of subcritical powers
statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ have finite measure, $1\le q<r<\infty$, $m\ge1$, and $u_j\to u$ in $L^q(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with $\sup_j\|u_j\|_r<\infty$. Then $u\in L^r(\Omega)$ and, for every $1\le s<r/m$, $|u_j|^{m-1}u_j\to |u|^{m-1}u$ in $L^s(\Omega)$. The range is nonempty only when $m<r$; the endpoint $s=r/m$ is not asserted.
strategy: This is a locally derived nonlinear consequence of the sourced compactness/interpolation mechanism, not a quoted theorem. The published a.e.-subsequence corollary gives representatives converging a.e. along a subsequence; Fatou yields $\|u\|_r\le\sup_j\|u_j\|_r$. The full difference sequence is uniformly bounded in $L^r$. For $t=ms<r$, finite-measure Holder gives $L^t$ convergence if $t\le q$; otherwise Lyapunov interpolation between $q$ and $r$ gives it. For $m>1$, the scalar mean-value theorem implies $||a|^{m-1}a-|b|^{m-1}b|\le m(|a|^{m-1}+|b|^{m-1})|a-b|$; Holder with exponents $m/(m-1)$ and $m$ gives $\|N(u_j)-N(u)\|_s\le m(\|u_j\|_{ms}^{m-1}+\|u\|_{ms}^{m-1})\|u_j-u\|_{ms}\to0$. For $m=1$ use $N(u)=u$. Countable Choice is inherited through the representative extraction and Fatou interfaces.

title: A bounded map into $H^1_0$ yields a compact $L^2$ operator
statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded open set and $T:L^2(\Omega)\to H^1_0(\Omega)$ a bounded linear operator. Then $\iota T:L^2(\Omega)\to L^2(\Omega)$ is compact, where $\iota:H^1_0(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega)$ is inclusion. No boundary regularity is needed.
strategy: Given a bounded sequence $f_j$ in $L^2$, boundedness of $T$ makes $Tf_j$ bounded in $H^1_0=W^{1,2}_0$. Apply the zero-boundary $L^p$ Rellich theorem at $p=2$ to obtain a subsequence convergent in $L^2$. The inclusion is bounded since the $L^2$ norm is part of the $H^1$ norm; hence the composition is bounded linear and the compact-operator criterion applies. The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the zero-boundary Rellich supplier. This abstracts the resolvent composition without imposing any elliptic equation.

title: Closed target constraints survive compact extraction
statement: Assume Countable and Dependent Choice. Let $X$ be a normed space with compact continuous inclusion $J:X\hookrightarrow L^p(\Omega)$, $1\le p<\infty$, and let $C\subseteq L^p(\Omega)$ be closed in norm. Every bounded sequence $u_j\in X$ with $Ju_j\in C$ admits a subsequence $Ju_{j_k}\to v$ in $L^p(\Omega)$ with $v\in C$. In particular this applies to any of this page's Rellich inclusions, with their stated domain, exponent and choice hypotheses. This statement does not assert that $v$ belongs to $X$ or that $C$ is weakly closed.
strategy: By the definition of compact inclusion and the metric compactness equivalence, select a target-norm-convergent subsequence of $Ju_j$. If its limit $v$ were outside $C$, openness of the complement would give a target-norm ball about $v$ disjoint from $C$, contradicting convergence and membership of each term in $C$. Thus the constraint survives extraction. Countable and Dependent Choice are the exact compactness-to-subsequence interface; in the concrete Rellich applications carry each theorem's inherited Axiom of Choice separately.

title: High frequencies destroy uniform translation control
statement: Let $1\le p<\infty$, $c_p=(\int_0^{2\pi}|\sin x|^p\,dx)^{-1/p}$, and $f_j(x)=c_p\mathbf1_{(0,2\pi)}(x)\sin(jx)$ on $\mathbb R$. Then $\|f_j\|_p=1$ and all supports lie in $[0,2\pi]$, but with $h_j=\pi/j\to0$ one has $\liminf_j\|f_j(\cdot+h_j)-f_j\|_p\ge2$. Hence boundedness and tightness do not imply uniform translation continuity or relative compactness in $L^p$.
strategy: The period decomposition and substitution $y=jx$ give the normalization. On $(0,2\pi-h_j)$, the shift reverses the sine sign, so the difference has magnitude $2c_p|\sin(jx)|$. The integral lost over the strip of length $h_j$ is at most $h_j$, so the pth power of the difference norm is at least $2^pc_p^p(\int_0^{2\pi}|\sin(jx)|^p-h_j)\to2^p$. Relative compactness would force uniform translation continuity by the A-page necessity lemma, a contradiction. Countable Choice is inherited only when invoking that necessity lemma; the displayed estimates themselves use no choice.

title: Critical bubbles converge weakly but not strongly
statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $1\le p<n$, $p^*=np/(n-p)$, and choose a nonzero real $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(B(0,1))$ with $\|\varphi\|_{p^*}=1$. On $\Omega=B(0,1)$ put $u_j(x)=j^{(n-p)/p}\varphi(jx)$. Then $u_j\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$, $\|u_j\|_{p^*}=1$, $\|Du_j\|_p=\|D\varphi\|_p$, and $\|u_j\|_p=j^{-1}\|\varphi\|_p$. Moreover $u_j\rightharpoonup0$ in $L^{p^*}$ and $u_j\to0$ a.e.; no subsequence converges strongly in $L^{p^*}$.
strategy: This is the smooth-profile version of Hunter Example 3.47 and Kinnunen Example 3.46, with the weak-limit assertion checked locally. Scaling gives all three norms. The supports shrink to the origin, so pointwise convergence holds away from that single null point. Since $p^*>1$, every real bounded linear functional on $L^{p^*}$ is integration against some $g\in L^{(p^*)\prime}$ by the published duality theorem. Holder gives $|\int u_jg|\le\|g\mathbf1_{B(0,1/j)}\|_{(p^*)\prime}\to0$ by dominated convergence. Any strong subsequential limit would be weakly zero and therefore zero, contradicting norm 1. Countable Choice is inherited through duality and dominated convergence.

title: Critical traces fail compactness under boundary dilation
statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<n$, $q_\partial=p(n-1)/(n-p)$, and let $\Omega$ be a bounded smooth domain having a flat boundary patch at the origin: locally $\Omega=\{x_n>0\}$ and $\partial\Omega=\{x_n=0\}$. Choose a smooth compactly supported profile $\psi$ on the closed half-space, supported in a sufficiently small patch, whose boundary restriction $g(x\prime)=\psi(x\prime,0)$ is nonzero. Put $u_j(x)=j^{(n-p)/p}\psi(jx)$ on $\Omega$ for sufficiently large $j$. Then $(u_j)$ is bounded in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$, while its traces have fixed positive $L^{q_\partial}(\partial\Omega)$ norm and converge to zero at every boundary point except the origin. The critical trace inclusion is not compact even on such a domain.
strategy: This is a locally checked sharpness witness using the sourced trace scaling, not a quoted trace counterexample. Choose any bounded smooth domain with a flat patch, obtainable by smoothly joining a planar disk to a cap, and take the profile supported where the flat description holds. The bulk gradient scales by $j^{(n-p)/p+1-n/p}=1$ and the bulk Lp norm by $j^{-1}$. For the trace, (n-1)-dimensional change of variables gives $\|\gamma u_j\|_{q_\partial}=j^{(n-p)/p-(n-1)/q_\partial}\|g\|_{q_\partial}=\|g\|_{q_\partial}>0$. For smooth functions the published trace operator agrees with boundary restriction. Supports shrink to the origin. If a subsequence converged strongly at the critical boundary exponent, the published a.e.-subsequence theorem on surface measure would identify its limit with zero, contradicting the fixed norm. This disproves any general compactness claim at the critical exponent; the Axiom of Choice is inherited through the trace interface.

title: Expanding bumps lose tightness
statement: Let $1\le p<\infty$ and let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfy $\|\varphi\|_p=1$. Put $f_j(x)=j^{-n/p}\varphi(x/j)$. Then $\|f_j\|_p=1$, $\|Df_j\|_p=j^{-1}\|D\varphi\|_p$, and for every fixed $R$, $\int_{B(0,R)}|f_j|^p\to0$ and $\int_{|x|>R}|f_j|^p\to1$. The family is uniformly translation continuous but not tight or relatively compact in $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$.
strategy: Scaling gives the two norms. The mass in a fixed ball is $\int_{B(0,R/j)}|\varphi(y)|^pdy\le\|\varphi\|_\infty^p|B(0,R/j)|\to0$. Direct integration along segments gives $\|\tau_h f_j-f_j\|_p\le |h|j^{-1}\|D\varphi\|_p\le|h|\|D\varphi\|_p$. Finally, $f_j\to0$ uniformly on each fixed ball; any Lp convergent subsequence would converge in Lp on each ball and hence have global limit zero, contrary to its constant unit norm. This is dilation escape, with the noncompactness proof independent of a criterion or a choice principle.
